requirements.requirement: Validate every wire document structurally and then semantically.
Assert RFC 3339, URI, and URI Template formats.
A complete Snapshot has exactly one root identified by collection.rootNodeId.
Live IDs are unique and do not overlap Tombstone target IDs.
Parent and Alias graphs are acyclic and every parent has a structural kind.
Sibling positions are non-empty, unique, and compared as ASCII tokens.
Subject, Relation, Alias, Parent, and Provenance references resolve in collection scope.
Unknown core fields are rejected and extension data uses HTTPS namespace keys.
Unsafe executable Bookmark URL schemes are rejected.
A publication Mount declares directory, collection, and snapshot endpoints.
Clients follow declared endpoints and never infer object paths.
Endpoint templates are absolute Level 1 templates with exact registered variables.
Snapshot page cursors bind revision, principal, query scope, and page size.
Clients atomically replace state only after complete ordered Snapshot assembly.
Representation ETags include projection, query, content negotiation, and page identity.
Authorization-varying responses are private no-store and vary by Authorization.
Errors use RFC 9457 Problem Details with a stable machine code.
Anonymous discovery excludes unlisted collections.
Query parameters use registered decoding and reject unknown or duplicate scalar parameters.
Core Feed event types use exact discriminated data contracts.
Feed cursors are scoped, exclusive, opaque, and separate from Sync cursors.
Feed projections never expose private sidecars, credentials, native IDs, or unsafe extensions.
Existing-resource writes require If-Match and return 428 or 412 on precondition failure.
Retryable POST operations bind idempotency keys to principal, endpoint, and canonical request digest.
Collection and root creation commit atomically.
Annotation, Attachment, and Relation CRUD map to complete canonical Operations.
Publisher DELETE responses use Deletion Receipts that do not require or fabricate Sync cursors.
A Sync Session binds one Principal to one Collection, except for the constrained instance-scoped create_collection bootstrap.
Terminal results consume continuous Replica sequences, deferred results block the current sequence, and exact retries return the persisted original result.
Resource-specific typed updates carry base and incoming values and cannot address fields outside the corresponding HTTP write DTO.
Business state, Operation, Sequence Receipt, Conflict, Cursor, Audit, and Outbox commit or roll back in one transaction.
Pull returns Operation and Conflict events in authoritative commit order.
Sync Tombstones purge only after retention, active Replica acknowledgement, purge-boundary advancement, and durable deletion watermarks.
Instance-scoped bootstrap accepts only one atomic create_collection operation and binds the successful Session to the generated Collection.
Every Sync Tombstone contains a deleteCursor while Publisher Deletion Receipts remain cursor-independent.
Replica leases follow the active, expired, recovery_required, and retired state machine and retired Replica IDs never reactivate.
Effective authorization intersects credential scopes, object policy, and ancestor policies.
Server, Collection, ancestor, and object policies are always intersected in order without an inheritance bypass; explicit deny takes precedence and descendants cannot widen access.
JSON parsing rejects duplicate members, unsafe integers, and prototype-polluting keys.
Rate limits combine credential, IP, and instance ceilings and expose RFC 9651 fields.
The synthetic public principal matches only anonymous requests and is never added to an authenticated identity set.
Logical Resource URIs use the stable server UUID and unique metadata, Snapshot, and Node paths.
Every Tool has a validated input schema and write Tools return structured output.
Nested generic operations are assessed at their highest expanded risk.
High-risk actions use typed Plan operations and server-bound out-of-band approval.
MCP Tool results never return API key secrets to model context.
MCP read mounts expose the MCP endpoint and Resources capability, while read-only Tools remain optional.
MCP write mounts expose Tools and retain their mcp-read and publisher profile dependencies.
